Site of Mongmyeoksan Beacon Mound was the final destination for beacon signals sent from the border areas during Joseon. In the daytime, smoke was used to transmit messages, while at night a signal fire was lit. One beacon signal was at a time of calm and peace, but in the case of emergencies such as an uprising, the number of beacon signals was varied from 2 to 5 to indicate the urgency of the situation. This beacon platform was built in 1423 and survived intact for over 450 years until 1895. The current mound was restored in 1993.

This is a large and flat rock found west of the Sajik Park in Sajik-dong, Jongno-gu. In the early 16th century during the Joseon Dynasty, Jungjongbanjeong (insurrection of King Jungjong) resulted in the accession of Jungjong to the throne. At the time the Queen of Jungjong was the daughter of Sin Su-geun, who was killed during the insurrection, and the subordinates who supported King Jungjong demanded that the Queen be dethroned as she was the daughter of a criminal. King Jungjong had no choice but to dethrone the Queen and make her return to her home. He could not forget the joyful memories of their time spent together over the course of 10 years, so he often went to Gyeonghoeru to observe her home on the foothills of Inwangsan Mountain. Upon learning of this, she hung her dress on one of the highest rocks in Inwangsan Mountain that could be observed from Gyeonghoeru. This story was passed on to the people, and later they began calling the rock where the dethroned queen hung her dress, Chimabawi Rock.

Donuimun, which is also called Seodaemun (West Gate), used to be located at this site. In the 4th year of the reign of King Sejong (1422), during construction work to reduce the size of certain sections of the wall, Seojeonmun was closed and Donuimun was newly built at the current location. Since then, Donuimun has also been called Saemun or Sinmun (New Gate), while the nearby street was named Sinmunno after the gate. However, in 1915, during the Japanese occupation, when the streetcar service passed via the gate, the gate was dismantled and its building materials sold off. Currently, a public art work titled ¡°Invisible Gate¡± stands on the former Site of Donuimun.

Sukjeongmun, situated on the north side of the wall, is the only remaining gate whose sides are still connected with the wall. Built in 1976, the gate tower was an entirely new addition to the wall.  In Asia, the north traditionally represents shadows, darkness, and femininity, while the south represents light, masculinity, and brightness. Regarding the topography of Seoul, the north side of the city is characterized by hillside and the south side is low-lying ground, so it is said that yin, or feminine, energy is stronger. Thus, Sukjeongmun, the north gate usually remained closed except in times of severe drought.   There was also a popular saying that if Sukjeongmun was opened, the local women would become lustful. In the Chines Classic mulberry was often referred to the dating place. Coincidentally, there were some facilities related to mulberry outside Sukjeongmun such as Seonjamdan, being used to pray for a rich silkworm harvest. It might be one of the reason that people referred Sukjeongmun to those sayings.

Sungnyemun, also known as Namdaemun (South Gate), is the main gate of Seoul City Wall thas has been designated as National Treasure No. 1. Construction of the gate started in 1395 and ended in 1398, although it was rebuilt on two occasions in 1448 and 1479. In 1907, the right and left sides of the wall were demolished for the reason of causing inconvenience to the traffic, but the gate itself remained as a cultural heritage. I had been the oldest building in Seoul until February 2008, when the wooden structure on the second floor of the gate tower was burned down by fire. It was not fully restored until May 2013. In addition, an 83m-long section of wall connecting to both sides of Sungnyemun was restored at this time. It is a 2-story building with an arch-shaped hongyemun built at the center of the shaft base, and 5 front faces and 2 side faces. The roof, when seen from the front, has a trapezoidal shape and in Korean this type of is called Ujingakjibung. The name Sungnyemun is written vertically so that the two characters, Sung and Ye, are on top of each other and appear as though there is an intense fire burning. This was to prevent the fire energy of Gwanaksan Mountain from reaching inside the city wall by overpowering it with a greater fire.

Changuimun, situated on the northwest section of the wall, between mounts Inwangsan and Baegak, is the only auxiliary gate of which the gate tower has survived to the present day. This gate tower was destroyed in 1592 during the war against Japan, and was reconstructed in 1741. Changuimun is now also known as Jahamun, since the scenery around the gate seems similar to that of scenic site Jahadong in Gaegyeong, the capital of Goryeo.  A phoenix is engraved on the front of Hongye (arched door similar to rainbow) on Changuimun, and another one is painted on the ceiling. However, there is a popular saying that they are not phoenixes but chickens. As the topography outside Changuimun resembles a centipede, the chickens are put on there as the natural enemy of centipede to keep the balance of surrounding topography.
